chunks.text: How-to · 6 min read · By The Muntin Desk

Agentic booking went live in Google's AI Mode this spring: the assistant reserves the table through OpenTable, Resy, or Tock. If you are not connected to a supported provider, the assistant books someone else.
In short
Google's AI Mode can complete a reservation inside the answer through OpenTable, Resy, or Tock, no website visit, no phone call.
If your tables are not bookable through a supported provider, the assistant books a restaurant whose tables are.
65% of diners prefer to book directly on a restaurant's own site, so own the repeat booking once the agent makes the first one.

Ask Google for “a table for six near Dupont with a patio, Friday at 7,” and the new AI Mode does not just list options, it can book one. Through OpenTable, Resy, and Tock, the assistant completes the reservation inside the answer. The diner never opens a website and never calls. That is convenient for them and decisive for you: if your tables aren’t bookable through a provider the assistant talks to, it books a restaurant whose tables are.

This is the same shift we covered in the AI Mode rebuild, the answer can now act , not just describe. For reservations, “act” means complete the booking. There are two jobs here, and most restaurants are set up for neither.
Job one: be bookable where the agent can reach you.

The agent can only finish a reservation it can see. A table that exists in a paper book by the host stand, or behind a “call us” line, is not a table the assistant can offer. Getting your inventory into OpenTable, Resy, or Tock is what makes you eligible for the agentic flow at all, it’s the difference between being a candidate and being skipped. Those platforms take a cut, and that math is real; but the cost of being un-bookable by the assistant is the whole reservation, every time it asks.
Job two: own the booking once the diner is yours.

65% of diners say they would rather book directly on a restaurant’s own website than through a third party. That is the leverage. The agent may make the first booking through a platform, but a diner who had a clean experience comes back through your own reservation link next time, no commission , and the guest relationship is yours to keep. A reservation link that is buried, slow, or broken on a phone hands that repeat booking right back to the platform you pay.

Where diners prefer to book a table, when they are given a clean choice. Sixty-five percent prefer to book directly on the restaurant's own website. Thirty-five percent prefer to book through a third-party platform like OpenTable, Resy, or Tock. The split is the operator's leverage: the agent makes the first booking through a platform, but the repeat booking is yours to win on your own site.

The agentic booking path in Google's AI Mode. Step one: the diner asks the assistant for a table. Step two: the assistant finds tables it can actually book, only restaurants connected to a supported provider. Step three: it completes the reservation through OpenTable, Resy, or Tock, inside the answer. Step four: phone-only restaurants are skipped, because the agent cannot dial a phone.
What to check this week.

Two things, both quick. First, confirm your reservations are live on a supported provider, not just a phone line, that’s your ticket into the agent’s shortlist. Second, open your own site on a phone and book a table yourself: if the reservation link is slow, hidden below the fold, or dumps you into a clunky third-party frame, the repeat booking you should own goes back to the platform. The reservation-recovery playbook in recovering reservations from Find a Table covers the fixes; the storefront health check and the G B P grader flag the broken paths before a diner finds them.

A decision tree the operator can walk to find out where the agentic booking flow breaks for their restaurant. Question one: are your tables live on a supported provider, OpenTable, Resy, or Tock, with real inventory, not just a phone line? If no, stop here; you are invisible to the agent, and nothing below this matters until you fix it. If yes, go on. Question two: are your menu and photos current on your Google Business Profile? If no, you may be in the candidate pool but you are a weak pick in a three-name answer; refresh the profile. If yes, go on. Question three: is your own reservation link above the fold on a phone, one tap to a real booking widget? If no, the agent still hands you the first booking, but the commission-free repeat booking leaks back to the platform; fix the mobile link. If yes to all three, you are bookable by the agent and built to keep the repeat. The order is the lesson: question one unlocks the agent, question three unlocks the commission-free repeat.
Agentic booking isn’t a threat to fight; it’s a flow to be in. Be bookable so the agent can hand you the first reservation, and own your own booking so you keep the second one.
Key takeaways
The agent can only book a table it can see, paper books and phone-only lines are invisible to it.
Being on OpenTable, Resy, or Tock is the ticket into the agent's shortlist, costs and all.
A reservation link that is slow or buried on mobile hands the repeat booking back to the platform.
Agentic booking is a flow to be in, not a threat to fight.
